newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says Mexico repayment vindicates U.S. aid.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says Mexico repayment vindicates U.S. aid.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday hailed Mexico's early repayment of its emergency U.S. loan, calling it a vindication of his decision to help the country out of its financial crisis two years ago.

At a White House ceremony, Clinton also said Mexico's announcement that it would repay the last $3.5 billion of $13.5 billion borrowed from the U.S. Treasury three years ahead of time was a tribute to the country's economic recovery.

The U.S. loans were part of a nearly $50 billion package crafted by the United States, the International Monetary Fund and other nations to avert a global financial disaster in the wake of Mexico's financial crisis in late 1994 and early 1995 that made financial markets around the world shudder.

"When my administration put together this emergency support package, Mexico was in crisis," Clinton said at the ceremony, which was attended by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.

"Today the United States is being repaid more than three years ahead of schedule, we have earned more than half a billion dollars on our loan, our exports to Mexico are at an all-time high and the Mexican economy is back on track."

The repayment was a sweet political victory for Clinton, who was harshly criticised for the loan package by many, including independent presidential candidate Ross Perot and Republican Pat Buchanan, who made a run for the White House.

"Two years ago helping our friend and neighbour in a time of need was quite controversial," Clinton added. "Some said that we should not get involved, that the money would never be repaid, that Mexico should fend for itself. They were wrong."

The massive loan package, which Mexico did not have to fully exploit, bought the country breathing room to cope with a cash squeeze brought on by its overspending on imports and its excessive reliance on short-term debt.
The liquidity crisis had brought Mexico to the brink of default on its loans and in early 1995 sent stock prices in developing countries from Latin America to Asia skidding lower in sympathy.

"We had to act to prevent the crisis destabilising our third largest trading partner, spreading to other emerging markets .... and threatening the sales of goods and services that generate jobs for American workers," Clinton said.
The nearly $50 billion package put together in January 1995 included up to $20 billion from the United States, $17.8 billion from the IMF and $10 billion from other industrial nations.

In announcing it would pay off the last $3.5 billion owed to the United States, Mexico also said it would make an early $1.5 billion payment to the IMF. Mexican officials said they would still owe the IMF about $10.5 billion after this.
U.S. officials said the wire transfer of the $3.5 billion would go through on Thursday. They also said the United States had overall earned $580 million in interest for the loan.

Clinton, clearly delighted at the Mexican news, said he hoped to visit the country soon. U.S. officials said later that a visit could take place in March or April, adding that Clinton could make the trip independent of a tour of Latin America that he has tentatively scheduled for the spring.
